\chapter{Green and Yellow}
\label{ch:ge-green-and-yellow}
\hlchaptermodality{23}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name green and yellow in German, and say why grün is English green's own cousin while gelb's link to French jaune is only probable.}

Say grün as the direct cousin of English green from a root unrelated to Latin viridis, say gelb, and state the gelb / jaune cousinhood as probable rather than airtight. The chapter's only lesson, so the payoff covers everything it introduces.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[grün, gelb]{grün, gelb — English's own cousin, and a secret cousin of French}

\label{lesson:GE-C23-gruen-gelb}



\begin{quote}
German's green word is a direct cousin of English's own word. Its yellow word has a cousin too — but a much more surprising one, sitting inside French.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{grün} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{green}\textquotedblright{}) is native Germanic, from Proto-Germanic \emph{\textbf{*grōniz}}, ultimately from \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{*ǵ\textsuperscript{h}reh\textsubscript{1}-}}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to grow, to become green}\textquotedblright{} — the \textbf{exact same root} as English's own \textbf{green}. Be careful, though: this is a \textbf{completely different} root from Latin's \textbf{viridis} (source of Spanish's \emph{verde}, French's \emph{vert}), which traces to its own, separate \textquotedblleft{}to grow/flourish\textquotedblright{} root, \emph{\textbf{*weis-}}. Two unrelated language families each independently built a \textquotedblleft{}green\textquotedblright{} word out of a verb meaning \textquotedblleft{}to grow\textquotedblright{} — a real coincidence of logic, not a shared word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{gelb} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{yellow}\textquotedblright{}) is native too, from Proto-Germanic \emph{\textbf{*gelwaz}} — and the same word as English's \textbf{yellow}. Trace it back far enough, to \textbf{Proto-Indo-European} \emph{\textbf{*ghel-}} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to shine},\textquotedblright{} with derivatives covering yellow, green, and gold), and it is usually said to land on the \textbf{same ancient root} behind Latin's \textbf{galbus/galbinus} — the source of \textbf{French}'s \textbf{jaune}. Honesty check, though: that particular link is \textbf{less secure} than it looks — some modern Latin scholarship treats \emph{galbus}'s origin as genuinely unknown rather than confirming the \emph{*ghel-} connection. So \emph{gelb} and \emph{jaune} are \textbf{probably} PIE-level cousins, despite belonging to completely different language families and reaching German and French by entirely separate paths — just don't treat the link as airtight.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}grün\textquotedblright{} — green, direct cousin of English's own \textquotedblleft{}green\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gelb\textquotedblright{} — yellow, probable hidden cousin of French's jaune
  \item the contrast — grün's root is unrelated to Latin's viridis, but gelb's root is PROBABLY shared with French's jaune
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{grün} related to Latin's \emph{viridis}? (\textbf{No} — a completely different root, though both independently mean \textquotedblleft{}grow\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}green\textquotedblright{}; \emph{grün} IS a direct cousin of English's own \textquotedblleft{}green.\textquotedblright{}) What French word is \textbf{gelb}'s probable PIE cousin, and how solid is that link? (\textbf{Jaune} — both usually traced to PIE \emph{*ghel-}, \textquotedblleft{}to shine,\textquotedblright{} though modern Latin scholarship treats \emph{galbus}'s origin as genuinely unknown, so the connection is probable, not certain.)
\end{tcolorbox}
